Figure 1:Goal grounding is key to object-goal navigation.(a, b)Baselinesexplore as well asoursyet walk past the goal; ours stops within 0.25 m.(c)Our system has explicit goal grounding, which enables the agent
to stop at the right place.(d)Ours has the highest success rate of all compared systems on sixcleanedbenchmarks.(e)Success rate against the rate of reaching the goal vicinity.
All baselines reach the vicinity far more often than they succeed.

Figure 4:System overview.The perception model writes grounding text for each frame. The policy
reads the frames interleaved with this text and outputs the next action.
The two models are trained separately, both on grounding text from the
scene annotations.

Figure 5:Two defects of the evaluation.(a) The same object type is annotated under many names, and only the
exact annotated name earns success credit. (b) The annotations contain
errors of two kinds, and a manual audit filters out 23% of the
val_unseen episodes.

Figure 6:Same episode, different decisions.(a) Paths of both systems through the scene. (b) Views at each system’s closest approach to the goal and at itsSTOP, labeled with the step and the action taken. Our frames also show the predicted grounding. (c) Goal distance of both systems, with our predicted goal visibility, distance bin, and stop probability. Steps 30 to 64 are enlarged.

Figure 8:Perception errors of our system.Top, examples of each error type. (a) Final-system failures on OVON val_unseen by cause. (b) Final-system success per goal category against how often the perception model reports the goal in view.
